    Your best adds

    Adds are ranked by the gain to your starters in DDF value, with the drop that costs your roster the least; bench players are not counted in that gain. Each card’s verdict (Pick up, Pick up (force), Consider, Hold, Skip) uses the “with bench” figure against a small noise margin, so a card can be ranked by its starter gain and judged on its with-bench gain. The “with bench” figure also counts your bench at the bench weight, as Team’s best move does, so Team can show a different gain for the same add.       Adjusted curve view

      • Shared scale. Every published chart is indexed to the same total value pie before comparison.
      • Our weighting. Adjusted curves shift position and roster-depth weighting toward our view of value rather than preserving each publisher's systematic lean.
      • Common adjustments. The main targets are tight-end overweighting, bench overweighting, and mismatched replacement-level assumptions.

      How should I read the curves?

      Every line uses the same scoring-specific trade-value scale. Player rank runs left to right; trade value runs bottom to top. Starter, bench, and waiver lines are vertical rank boundaries under every lock. No median, average, or blended composite curve is plotted.

      Solid lines are as-published values reindexed to the shared scale plus ESPN’s projection-derived series. Dashed adjusted lines shift the weighting to our view of value. Missing values break that source’s line rather than becoming zero.

      Take your setup with you

      Export a versioned JSON file with league settings, view, filters, and each source's selected edition. Imported files from a different weekly snapshot pause for confirmation before they change anything.

      How we make the charts comparable

      Every publisher's chart has habits — small, consistent leans in how they value players. We measure those habits against our own ESPN-based view of value and adjust for them, so when two lines disagree about a player, it's a real disagreement about the player, not a difference in house style. Everything below follows your league settings.

      1 One pie, same scale

      First, every chart is rescaled to the same total value at your league settings, so a 40 means the same thing everywhere. Each publisher still slices that pie their own way:

      2 Our view starts from ESPN's projections

      Our adjusted view isn't another opinion — it's built from ESPN's season projections. We turn ESPN's per-game projections into value above waivers: each position gets a fixed share of total value, split 85% to starters and 15% to the bench. Where the starter line falls depends on your league — with 12 teams and 2 starting running backs, the 24th RB is the last starter; with 10 teams, it's the 20th. Players projected below the waiver line are worth nothing; everyone above it earns value based on how far above that line they sit.

      3 Each chart is recalibrated toward that view

      For each publisher, we compare their published values against our ESPN-based view and fit a correction per position — separately for starters and bench. A publisher whose starting running backs run hot gets cooled; one whose bench receivers are undervalued gets a lift. It's not simply "move value from RBs to WRs" — it's a per-position, per-tier recalibration, and because the starter and bench lines move with your league settings, the corrections move too. Pick a chart to see its biggest adjustments at your current settings:

      Notes & source definitions
      1. Scale and missing values. Every series is put on one shared trade-value scale for your league settings. A missing or unpriced value shows as — and is never converted to zero; a value of 0 means the player is at or below that source’s waiver line.
      2. Series taxonomy. As-published values are reindexed only onto the common scoring-specific scale. FC Adjusted, USAT Adjusted, FP Adjusted, and CBS Adjusted are adjusted best-estimate values that shift the weighting to our view of value; a missing adjusted value shows as —.
      3. Sources. USA Today is an editorial chart; FantasyCalc reflects completed fantasy trades; FantasyPros is an analyst-consensus chart; CBS is an editorial chart; ESPN uses its season projections translated to the same scale.
      4. Freshness. Content date is when a source's published numbers last changed; fit date identifies the bias-adjustment bake. Each published chart is labeled with the week it covers, and a chart from an older week is marked and starts switched off. ESPN projections are pulled daily.
